title: Semaglutide as a therapeutic option for elderly patients with type 2 diabetes: Pooled analysis of the SUSTAIN 1-5 trials

citation.title: Semaglutide as a therapeutic option for elderly patients with type 2 diabetes: Pooled analysis of the SUSTAIN 1-5 trials

printed_heading.text: BRIE F R EP ORT Semaglutide as a therapeutic option for elderly patients with type 2 diabetes: Pooled analysis of the SUSTAIN 1-5 trials Mark Warren MD1 | Louis Chaykin MD2 | David Trachtenbarg MD3 | Gurudutt Nayak MD4 | Nelun Wijayasinghe MD4 | Bertrand Cariou MD5 1 Physicians East, Greenville, North Carolina 2 Meridien Research, Bradenton, Florida 3 University of Illinois College of Medicine at Peoria, Peoria, Illinois 4 Novo Nordisk A/S, Søborg, Denmark 5 L'Institut du Thorax, Department of Endocrinology, CHU de Nantes, Nantes, France Correspondence Mark Warren, MD, FACE, Department of Endocrinology and Metabolism, Physicians East, 1006 WH Smith Blvd, Greenville, NC 27834. Email: mwarren@physicianseast.com Funding information This study and the associated trials were supported by Novo Nordisk A/S, Denmark. The efficacy and safety of semaglutide vs comparators in non-elderly (<65 years) and elderly (≥65 years) patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) across the SUSTAIN 1-5 trials were evaluated. Patients were randomized to once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide (0.5 or 1.0 mg) vs placebo, sitagliptin, exenatide or insulin. The primary objective was change in HbA1c and secondary objectives were changes in body weight and safety. Mean HbA1c decreased from baseline by 1.2%-1.5% and 1.5%-1.9% vs 0%-0.9% (non-elderly, n = 3045) and by 1.3%-1.5% and 1.2%- 1.8% vs 0.2%-1.0% (elderly, n = 854) with semaglutide 0.5 and 1.0 mg vs comparators. Similar reductions from baseline in mean body weight with semaglutide occurred in both age groups. Similar proportions of patients experienced adverse events; premature treatment discontinuations were higher in elderly vs non-elderly patients. No increased risk of severe or blood glucose-confirmed hypoglycaemia was seen with semaglutide vs comparators between age groups. Semaglutide had a comparable efficacy and safety profile in non-elderly and elderly patients across the SUSTAIN 1-5 trials, making it an effective treatment option for elderly patients with T2D. KEYWORDS antidiabetic drug, GLP-1 analogue, glycaemic control, incretin therapy, type 2 diabetes 1 | INTRODUCTION The incidence of type 2 diabetes (T2D) increases with age, reaching a peak at 65-69 years for men and 75-79 years for women.1 It is therefore important that safe and effective treatments are available for elderly patients with T2D. The primary objective was to assess the effect of semaglutide on glycaemic control (change in HbA1c in patients with T2D) at the end of treatment (EOT).
The post hoc analysis assessed outcomes in non-elderly (<65 years) and elderly (≥65 years) patients, pooled by age group (Appendix S1).

reported_results.text: Treatment differences between age groups were not significant (except for SUSTAIN 2, P = 0.02) (Figure S2). 3.3 | Safety Pooled data showed that in patients receiving semaglutide 0.5 mg, 1.0 mg and comparators, the proportion of patients experiencing AEs was comparable between the two age groups.

HbA1c <8% was achieved by 90%-100% of elderly patients treated with semaglutide 0.5 mg, and 85%-97% of elderly patients treated with semaglutide 1.0 mg, vs 47%-85% treated with comparators. 3.2 | Body weight Semaglutide consistently reduced mean BW from baseline to EOT in both groups vs comparators (Figure 1B).

Tests for homogeneity of treatment effects were all non-significant, except for SUSTAIN 4 where more non-elderly patients treated with semaglutide 1.0 mg reached this target vs elderly patients (P = 0.01) (Figure S1).
